heterocycles-biomolecules-001.question: Which statement about the lone pair on the nitrogen atom of pyridine, C5H5N, is correct?
choices: It occupies a nitrogen p orbital and is part of the aromatic 6π-electron system, so it hardly binds a proton
It occupies an in-plane sp² orbital outside the aromatic 6π system, so it can accept a proton
It occupies an sp³ hybrid orbital, and the nitrogen has the same pyramidal geometry as in ammonia
heterocycles-biomolecules-001.explanation: In pyridine all six ring atoms are sp² hybridized, and their p orbitals hold one electron each, six π electrons in all, satisfying Hückel's rule (4n + 2, n = 1); pyridine is aromatic. The nitrogen contributes one electron to this p orbital, and its lone pair stays in an sp² orbital pointing out in the plane of the ring. It can therefore accept a proton without losing aromaticity, and pyridine behaves as a weak base whose pyridinium ion C5H5NH⁺ has a pKa of about 5.2. A lone pair in a p orbital that is part of the π system is a feature of the nitrogen of pyrrole, not pyridine. The nitrogen of pyridine is part of a planar ring, not an sp³ pyramid.

heterocycles-biomolecules-002.question: Pyrrole, C4H4NH, is a much weaker base than pyridine, C5H5N (conjugate acid pKa about 5.2); the pKa of its conjugate acid is about −4. What is the main reason?
choices: The nitrogen is sp hybridized, so its lone pair is held tightly by the nucleus
The hydrogen of the N−H bond gets in the way sterically, so a proton cannot approach the nitrogen
The nitrogen lone pair is built into the aromatic 6π-electron system, so protonating it destroys the aromaticity
heterocycles-biomolecules-002.explanation: The nitrogen of pyrrole is sp² hybridized, and the four π electrons of the four carbons plus the two electrons of the lone pair in the nitrogen p orbital make up an aromatic 6π-electron system. Giving this pair to a proton would break the 6π system and lose the aromatic stabilization, so the nitrogen hardly acts as a base at all. In strong acid, protonation actually occurs on a ring carbon (position 2), and the pKa of that conjugate acid is about −4. The nitrogen is not sp hybridized (sp nitrogen is found in nitriles), and the N−H hydrogen is small, so it causes no steric hindrance to protonation. Whether the lone pair is part of the π system is what separates the basicity of pyridine and pyrrole.

heterocycles-biomolecules-003.question: Which of the following compounds is aromatic according to Hückel's rule?
choices: Furan, C4H4O
1,3-Cyclopentadiene, C5H6
Cyclooctatetraene, C8H8
heterocycles-biomolecules-003.explanation: To be aromatic, a molecule must be cyclic and planar, every ring atom must have a p orbital in conjugation, and there must be 4n + 2 π electrons. In furan the four carbons supply four electrons and one of the two lone pairs on oxygen sits in a p orbital and supplies two, for a total of six π electrons (n = 1), so furan is aromatic. The other lone pair occupies an sp² orbital in the plane of the ring. In 1,3-cyclopentadiene the CH2 carbon is sp³ hybridized and breaks the conjugation around the ring, so it is not aromatic (the anion C5H5⁻ formed by losing H⁺ has six π electrons and is aromatic). Cyclooctatetraene has eight π electrons (4n), and it is not planar but tub-shaped, so it is not aromatic.

heterocycles-biomolecules-004.question: Imidazole, C3H4N2, has a conjugate acid pKa of about 7.0 and is a stronger base than pyridine (about 5.2). Which combination of the site of protonation and the reason it is more basic than pyridine is correct?
choices: The pyrrole-type nitrogen bearing the N−H is protonated, removing the repulsion between the lone pairs of the two nitrogens
The pyridine-type nitrogen without N−H is protonated, and resonance spreads the positive charge over both nitrogens
Both nitrogens are protonated at once, and the resulting dication is strongly stabilized by hydration with the surrounding water molecules
heterocycles-biomolecules-004.explanation: Of the two nitrogens in imidazole, the lone pair of the N−H nitrogen at position 1 is built into the 6π aromatic system, while the lone pair of the nitrogen at position 3, which has no N−H, sits in an sp² orbital as in pyridine and acts as the base. The imidazolium ion formed by protonation at position 3 is a symmetric cation with two N−H groups; resonance spreads the positive charge over both nitrogens and aromaticity is kept, so it is stable. This is why the conjugate acid pKa is about 7.0, making imidazole more basic than pyridine. Protonation of the pyrrole-type nitrogen would destroy aromaticity and is unfavorable, and the dication hardly forms in ordinary aqueous solution. This property is also why the histidine side chain (pKa about 6.0) acts as an acid–base catalyst near physiological pH.

heterocycles-biomolecules-005.question: Which ordering of piperidine (CH2)5NH, pyridine C5H5N and pyrrole C4H4NH from strongest to weakest base (largest to smallest conjugate acid pKa) is correct?
choices: Pyridine > piperidine > pyrrole
Pyrrole > pyridine > piperidine
Piperidine > pyridine > pyrrole
heterocycles-biomolecules-005.explanation: The conjugate acid pKa values are about 11.1 for piperidine, a saturated cyclic secondary amine, about 5.2 for pyridine and about −4 for pyrrole. The nitrogen lone pair of piperidine is in an sp³ orbital (25% s character), held less tightly by the nucleus than the sp² orbital of pyridine (33% s character), so it is more readily given to a proton and piperidine is the strongest base. Pyridine is aromatic, but its lone pair is not part of the π system, so it is a moderately weak base. Pyrrole is the weakest because its lone pair is built into the aromatic 6π system. Ranking pyridine as the strongest confuses aromatic stability with basicity, and ranking pyrrole as the strongest wrongly treats it like an amine just because it has an N−H.

heterocycles-biomolecules-006.question: When glycine, H2NCH2COOH, is dissolved in water near neutrality (pH about 6), which form is mainly present?
choices: The zwitterion H3N⁺CH2COO⁻
The uncharged neutral molecule H2NCH2COOH
The cation H3N⁺CH2COOH
heterocycles-biomolecules-006.explanation: The pKa of glycine's carboxy group is about 2.3, and that of the ammonium group −NH3⁺ is about 9.6. A pH of about 6 is well above the pKa of the carboxy group, so almost all −COOH becomes −COO⁻, and well below the pKa of the ammonium group, so −NH3⁺ remains. The main form is therefore the zwitterion H3N⁺CH2COO⁻, with one positive and one negative charge and a net charge of zero. The uncharged molecule H2NCH2COOH is a tautomer of this zwitterion, but its proportion in water is tiny. The cation H3N⁺CH2COOH predominates only in acidic solutions below a pH of about 2.3. Amino acids have high melting points, dissolve readily in water and poorly in organic solvents because they exist as zwitterions even in the solid.

heterocycles-biomolecules-007.question: Take the pKa values of glycine as 2.34 for the carboxy group and 9.60 for the ammonium group. What is the isoelectric point pI of glycine?
heterocycles-biomolecules-007.explanation: The isoelectric point is the pH at which the net charge of an amino acid is zero, and it is found as the average of the pKa values of the two dissociation steps on either side of the net-zero form (the zwitterion). Glycine dissociates in two steps, cation H3N⁺CH2COOH ⇌ zwitterion H3N⁺CH2COO⁻ ⇌ anion H2NCH2COO⁻, so pI = (pKa1 + pKa2)/2 = (2.34 + 9.60)/2 = 5.97. At this pH, small and equal amounts of the cation and anion are present, and nearly everything is the zwitterion. 11.94 is the sum without dividing by 2, and 3.63 is the difference (9.60 − 2.34) divided by 2; neither matches the definition of pI. At the isoelectric point a molecule does not move in electrophoresis and its solubility tends to be low, facts used in separating proteins.

heterocycles-biomolecules-008.question: Take the pKa values of aspartic acid, HOOCCH2CH(NH2)COOH, as 1.88 for the α-carboxy group, 3.65 for the side-chain carboxy group and 9.60 for the ammonium group. What is the isoelectric point pI of aspartic acid?
heterocycles-biomolecules-008.explanation: For an amino acid with an acidic side chain, use the pKa values of the two steps on either side of the form with zero net charge (α-COO⁻, side-chain COOH, NH3⁺). From the fully protonated +1 form, the α-carboxy group (1.88) loses its proton first to give the net-zero form, and then the side-chain carboxy group (3.65) loses its proton to give the −1 form. Therefore pI = (1.88 + 3.65)/2 = 2.765 ≈ 2.77. 5.04 is the average of all three pKa values, and 6.63 is the average of the side chain and ammonium group, (3.65 + 9.60)/2, a mistake that picks the steps on either side of the −1 form. Acidic amino acids have low pI values, so they are negatively charged near neutral pH.

heterocycles-biomolecules-009.question: A mixture of glycine (pI 5.97), aspartic acid (pI 2.77) and lysine (pKa 2.18 for the α-carboxy group, 8.95 for the α-ammonium group and 10.53 for the side-chain ammonium group) was subjected to electrophoresis in a pH 6.0 buffer. Which one moves toward the cathode (negative electrode)?
choices: Glycine
Lysine
Aspartic acid
heterocycles-biomolecules-009.explanation: For lysine, with its basic side chain, the steps on either side of the net-zero form are those of the α-ammonium group (8.95) and the side-chain ammonium group (10.53), so pI = (8.95 + 10.53)/2 = 9.74. An amino acid is positively charged when the pH is below its pI and negatively charged when the pH is above it. pH 6.0 is below lysine's pI of 9.74, so lysine is positively charged and moves toward the cathode. Aspartic acid is at a pH above its pI of 2.77, so it is negatively charged and moves toward the anode, and glycine, whose pI of 5.97 is almost equal to the pH, has nearly zero net charge and hardly moves. The key points are that cations move toward the cathode and that the side-chain pKa must be included when finding the pI.

heterocycles-biomolecules-010.question: Which statement about the peptide bond (amide bond) −CO−NH− in proteins is correct?
choices: Resonance of the N lone pair with the carbonyl gives the C−N bond partial double-bond character, so the six atoms lie nearly in one plane and C−N rotation is restricted
The C−N bond has the same length as an ordinary single bond (about 1.47 Å) and rotates freely about its axis, which is why the protein backbone can bend and fold flexibly
The nitrogen is sp³ hybridized and pyramidal, and because its lone pair is freely available, the peptide nitrogen is about as strong a base as an amine
heterocycles-biomolecules-010.explanation: The lone pair on the amide nitrogen is delocalized by resonance with the carbonyl group (N−C=O ↔ N⁺=C−O⁻), and the C−N bond, at about 1.33 Å, is intermediate in length between a single bond (about 1.47 Å) and a double bond (about 1.27 Å). Because of this partial double-bond character, the six atoms Cα−C(=O)−N(H)−Cα lie nearly in one plane, rotation about C−N is hindered, and the sterically favored trans form is usually adopted. The flexibility of the backbone comes from rotation about the single bonds on either side of Cα (φ and ψ), not from free rotation about C−N. Also, because the lone pair is used in resonance, the amide nitrogen hardly acts as a base (protonation occurs instead on oxygen, with a conjugate acid pKa of about 0), very different from an amine.

heterocycles-biomolecules-011.question: Two molecules of glycine, H2NCH2COOH (molar mass 75.07 g/mol), and one molecule of alanine, CH3CH(NH2)COOH (molar mass 89.09 g/mol), condensed to form the tripeptide Gly-Ala-Gly. Taking the molar mass of water, H2O, as 18.02 g/mol, what is the molar mass of this tripeptide?
heterocycles-biomolecules-011.explanation: A peptide bond forms by condensation, with one molecule of water lost from the carboxy group of one amino acid and the amino group of another. A tripeptide linking three amino acids has two peptide bonds, so two molecules of water are lost. The molar mass is 2 × 75.07 + 89.09 − 2 × 18.02 = 239.23 − 36.04 = 203.19 g/mol (molecular formula C7H13N3O4). 239.23 g/mol simply adds the amino acids without subtracting water, and 221.21 g/mol subtracts only one water. In general, a linear peptide of n amino acids has n − 1 peptide bonds and loses n − 1 molecules of water. The same idea is used when estimating the molecular weight of a protein from the average residue mass.

heterocycles-biomolecules-012.question: In aqueous solution, D-glucose, C6H12O6, exists mainly as a six-membered ring (pyranose), in α and β forms. Which statement about these two forms is correct?
choices: They are enantiomers (mirror-image isomers), so their specific rotations are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign
They are diastereomers (anomers) differing only in the configuration at C1, and in water they interconvert through the open-chain form
They differ only in the orientation of the C5 hydroxy group, and once the ring forms they never reopen to the chain or interconvert in water
heterocycles-biomolecules-012.explanation: In the open-chain form of glucose, the hydroxy group at C5 adds intramolecularly to the aldehyde group at C1 to form a hemiacetal, giving a six-membered ring. C1 becomes a new stereocenter (the anomeric carbon), and the two orientations of its OH give the two anomers, α and β. They are diastereomers differing only at C1, and their specific rotations differ in magnitude as well: +112° for the α form and +18.7° for the β form. In water they interconvert through the ring-opened open-chain form, and the specific rotation drifts toward its equilibrium value (mutarotation). The enantiomer is L-glucose, in which every stereocenter is inverted. The configuration at C5 is the one that decides D or L and has nothing to do with α/β.

heterocycles-biomolecules-013.question: In water at 25 °C, take the specific rotation of α-D-glucopyranose as +112.2° and that of β-D-glucopyranose as +18.7°. An aqueous glucose solution reached equilibrium after mutarotation, with a specific rotation of +52.7°. If the proportion of the open-chain and other forms is negligible, which value is closest to the proportion of the β form at equilibrium?
heterocycles-biomolecules-013.explanation: The specific rotation is the average of the components weighted by their proportions. Letting x be the proportion of the β form, 112.2(1 − x) + 18.7x = 52.7, so x = (112.2 − 52.7)/(112.2 − 18.7) = 59.5/93.5 = 0.636. The β form therefore makes up about 64% and the α form about 36%. 36% is a mix-up that gives the proportion of the α form, and 47% is 52.7/112.2, dividing the equilibrium value by the value of the α form alone and ignoring the contribution of the β form. The β form predominates because in the chair conformation of β-D-glucopyranose all the ring substituents, including the OH at C1, are equatorial, so steric repulsion from 1,3-diaxial interactions is small.

heterocycles-biomolecules-014.question: Analysis of the base composition of a double-stranded DNA found that adenine, A, made up 30% of all bases (as a mole fraction). What proportion of this DNA is guanine, G?
heterocycles-biomolecules-014.explanation: In double-stranded DNA, purine and pyrimidine bases form fixed pairs by hydrogen bonding: adenine A pairs with thymine T through two hydrogen bonds, and guanine G pairs with cytosine C through three. Therefore A = T and G = C (Chargaff's rules). If A is 30%, T is also 30%, and G and C share the remaining 40% equally, so G is 20%. 30% mistakes A as equal to G, and 40% takes the sum of G and C as G alone. Because G−C pairs have three hydrogen bonds, the higher the proportion of G + C in a DNA, the higher the temperature at which the double strand comes apart (the melting temperature). In RNA, uracil U pairs with adenine in place of thymine.

heterocycles-biomolecules-015.question: What is the saponification value of tripalmitin, (C15H31COO)3C3H5 (the triester of three molecules of palmitic acid, C15H31COOH, with glycerol, C3H5(OH)3; molar mass 807.3 g/mol)? The saponification value is the mass (mg) of potassium hydroxide, KOH (molar mass 56.11 g/mol), needed to saponify 1 g of the fat.
heterocycles-biomolecules-015.explanation: A triglyceride molecule has three ester bonds, so three molecules of KOH are needed for saponification ((C15H31COO)3C3H5 + 3KOH → 3C15H31COOK + C3H5(OH)3). 1 g of tripalmitin is 1/807.3 mol, so the KOH needed is 3 × 56.11 × 1000/807.3 = 208.5 mg, and the saponification value is about 209. 69.5 counts only one molecule of KOH, and 149 calculates with the mass of NaOH (40.00 g/mol) instead of KOH. The saponification value is larger for fats whose constituent fatty acids have a smaller average molecular weight (shorter carbon chains). Together with the iodine value, which reflects the number of double bonds, it is a basic indicator of the properties of fats and oils.
